name: Yukos

summary.text: Yukos was a Russian oil company that a company controlled by Mikhail Khodorkovsky and his partners acquired in the 1995 loans-for-shares auction, with Khodorkovsky's bank Menatep processing the bids, and which grew into Russia's largest oil company. After Khodorkovsky's arrest in October 2003 the company was dismantled: its main production unit, Yuganskneftegaz, was sold at a state-run auction on December 19, 2004 to the previously unknown BaikalFinansGroup for about $9.3 billion, and state-owned Rosneft bought the buyer days later. The Moscow Arbitration Court declared Yukos bankrupt on August 1, 2006. An arbitral tribunal in The Hague awarded Yukos's former majority shareholders more than $50 billion against Russia in July 2014; Dutch courts set the awards aside in 2016, reinstated them in 2020, and after a partial remand by the Dutch Supreme Court in November 2021, that court dismissed Russia's final appeal on October 17, 2025.

facts.claim: In the 1995 loans-for-shares auction of Yukos, Khodorkovsky's bank Menatep processed the bids; the winner was a company controlled by Khodorkovsky and his partners, and a rival bid from three large Russian banks that offered more money was disqualified on technical grounds. Bloomberg reported in April 1996 that Menatep was putting up $350 million, about half the company's estimated worth; The Moscow Times then described Yukos as Russia's second-largest oil company, and RFE/RL says Khodorkovsky built it into Russia's largest.

facts.claim: Yukos's main production unit, Yuganskneftegaz, was sold on Sunday, December 19, 2004 at a state-run auction won by BaikalFinansGroup, a little-known company reported to be registered in Tver, for about $9.3 billion (reports range from just over $9 billion to $9.4 billion). Dresdner Kleinwort Wasserstein had valued the unit in an October 6, 2004 report at between $15.7 billion and $18.3 billion, and Yukos said it was worth more.

facts.claim: Days after the auction, state-owned Rosneft bought 100 percent of the shares in BaikalFinansGroup, according to news-agency reports cited by The Washington Post on December 22, 2004; a Rosneft spokesman confirmed the deal, saying the owners of Baikal had offered to sell their company and Rosneft took it.
facts.quote: Rosneft bought 100 percent of the shares in BaikalFinansGroup, according to news agency reports

sources.title: Russian Oil Firm Buys Mysterious Bid Winner

facts.claim: Yukos filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection in Houston before the auction. U.S. Bankruptcy Judge Letitia Clark granted a temporary injunction against the sale, after which Western banks froze financing for a Gazprom bid, but the Russian government held the auction anyway. Yukos then said it would seek $20 billion in damages from the buyers; the U.S. bankruptcy case was later dismissed for lack of jurisdiction.

facts.claim: On Tuesday, August 1, 2006 the Moscow Arbitration Court declared Yukos bankrupt; Judge Pavel Markov's decision upheld a vote by the company's creditors one week earlier, which was led by the Federal Tax Service and Rosneft. Yukos's lawyers said they would appeal.

facts.claim: RFE/RL summarised in 2016 that in the years after Khodorkovsky's arrest Yukos was dismantled, its key assets sold off in state-run auctions and acquired by the government-owned oil company Rosneft.

facts.claim: On July 18, 2014 an arbitral tribunal seated in The Hague under the auspices of the Permanent Court of Arbitration issued final awards in three cases begun in 2005 by Yukos's former majority shareholders, Hulley Enterprises, Yukos Universal and Veteran Petroleum, finding that Russia had breached the Energy Charter Treaty by destroying Yukos and taking its assets and ordering more than $50 billion in compensation, described as by far the largest award ever rendered by an arbitral tribunal. Interim awards on jurisdiction had been issued on November 30, 2009.

facts.claim: On April 20, 2016 the Hague District Court set aside the three interim awards of November 30, 2009 and the three final awards of July 18, 2014, holding that, based only on its signature of the Energy Charter Treaty, Russia was not bound by provisional application of the treaty's arbitration clause (Article 26) because Russian law confines arbitration to civil-law disputes; having upheld that first ground, the court did not consider Russia's four other grounds for annulment. The shareholders announced an appeal.
facts.quote: based only on the signature of the ECT, the Russian Federation was not bound by the provisional application of the arbitration regulations of Article 26 ECT

facts.claim: On February 18, 2020 the Hague Court of Appeal overturned the District Court's 2016 decision and reinstated the awards, worth a combined US$50 billion, holding that provisional application of Article 26 of the Energy Charter Treaty did not conflict with Russian law and rejecting all of Russia's other grounds for annulment. Russia appealed to the Dutch Supreme Court.
facts.quote: reinstated UNCITRAL awards worth a combined US$50 billion in favour of the oil company's former majority shareholders against Russia

facts.claim: On November 5, 2021 the Dutch Supreme Court set aside the Hague Court of Appeal's judgments in part: it held that the Court of Appeal had wrongly rejected on procedural grounds Russia's allegation that the shareholders had committed fraud in the arbitration, which should have been judged on its substance, and referred the case to the Amsterdam Court of Appeal; it rejected Russia's other grounds of appeal, including its complaints about the tribunal's jurisdiction and the interpretation and application of the Energy Charter Treaty.

facts.claim: The Amsterdam Court of Appeal ruled in 2024 that Russia's fraud allegation could not serve as a ground for annulling the awards, and on October 17, 2025 the Dutch Supreme Court dismissed Russia's final appeal, mainly on procedural grounds, in what its statement called a definitive end to the dispute, leaving the awards of more than $50 billion in favour of the former Yukos shareholders standing.

facts.claim: Enforcement proceedings on the awards were pursued in Belgium, France, Germany, the United Kingdom and the United States while the Dutch annulment case continued; in November 2023 the English High Court dismissed Russia's state-immunity challenge to enforcement in England. Law-firm commentary puts the sum due with accrued interest at about $57 billion or more.

openQuestions: Auction price: reports give about $9.3 billion, just over $9 billion, $9.35 billion and $9.4 billion for Yuganskneftegaz; the Dresdner Kleinwort Wasserstein valuation ($15.7-18.3 billion) was returned without its source being identified among the Washington Post, CBS and Moscow Times pages cited. The date of the U.S. dismissal of Yukos's Chapter 11 case (February 2005) is from the search summary.

Dutch Supreme Court 2023: no 2023 Supreme Court step on the annulment was found. The only 2023 item returned was an Advocate General's opinion of September 22, 2023 in a separate enforcement dispute over Russian vodka trademarks. The fraud question went from the Supreme Court (November 5, 2021) to the Amsterdam Court of Appeal (2024) and back to the Supreme Court (October 17, 2025). The Amsterdam Court of Appeal's 2024 judgment date was not captured.

Award totals: $50 billion is the principal of the July 2014 final awards (plus about $60 million in costs per one source); law-firm commentary gives about $57 billion or '$65+ billion' with interest. Pending enforcement proceedings by country are from 2016-2023 commentary and were not updated.

The passage describing the six awards (interim awards on jurisdiction of November 30, 2009 and final awards of July 18, 2014) and the 'largest award ever rendered' description were returned alongside several arbitration-law sources without a single one being identified; the Kluwer, IISD and Global Arbitration News pages are cited.

RFE/RL's 2011 piece 'Jailed Russian Official: Yukos Auction Was Staged' and the 2011 European Court of Human Rights hearing in Yukos's own application against Russia were listed in results but not opened. The tax claims brought against Yukos in 2003-2004 that preceded the auction were not researched.

The site frames Yukos as acquired through a Harvard HIID/USAID-designed scheme 'for virtually nothing'; the pages returned say Menatep put up $350 million (Bloomberg) or that the sale fetched $160 million (Moscow Times headline), and none connects the auction to HIID or USAID.
